proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(L_{\mathrm{bd}}<U_{\mathrm{bd}}\) and abbreviate \(\Delta=\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}=U_{\mathrm{bd}}-L_{\mathrm{bd}}>0\).  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}fixed\mbox{-}design\mbox{-}endpoint\mbox{-}reduction}\), specialized to the uniform law on \(\mathcal Z_n\), gives for every positive even \(n\)
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 =\Delta^2\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}. \tag{11}
\]
This is a minimax-value equality obtained by a labeled-data multilinear extension, not a claim that the pair of success counts is sufficient for nonbinary schedules.

Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}n24\mbox{-}equality}\) gives
\[
 \rho_2^{\mathrm{CR}}=\frac14,
 \qquad
 \rho_4^{\mathrm{CR}}=1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \tag{12}
\]
and Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}n6\mbox{-}seven\mbox{-}state\mbox{-}saddle}\) gives
\[
 \rho_6^{\mathrm{CR}}=s_6^2. \tag{13}
\]
Substitution of (12)--(13) into (11) proves the three exact bounded-class formulas in the statement.

We next compare these values with Hull's independent-design affine upper bound from Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}hull\mbox{-}independent\mbox{-}affine\mbox{-}upper}\).  At \(n=2\), \(\sqrt2>1\), and hence
\[
 \rho_2^{\mathrm{CR}}=\frac14>\frac1{(\sqrt2+1)^2}. \tag{14}
\]
At \(n=4\),
\[
 1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}>\frac19
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \sqrt3<\frac{16}{9}. \tag{15}
\]
Both sides of the last inequality are positive, and it follows by squaring because
\(
 3=243/81<256/81=(16/9)^2
\).  Since \((\sqrt4+1)^{-2}=1/9\), (15) is the required comparison.

At \(n=6\), the isolating interval in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}n6\mbox{-}algebraic\mbox{-}certificate}\) implies
\[
 s_6>\frac{29066256529188}{10^{14}}>\frac{29}{100}. \tag{16}
\]
Also \(\sqrt6>2449/1000\), since both sides are positive and
\[
 6>\frac{2449^2}{10^6}=\frac{5997601}{10^6}. \tag{17}
\]
Equations (16)--(17) give
\[
 s_6(\sqrt6+1)>
 \frac{29}{100}\frac{3449}{1000}
 =\frac{100021}{100000}>1.
\]
All quantities are positive, so squaring and dividing yields
\[
 \rho_6^{\mathrm{CR}}=s_6^2>\frac1{(\sqrt6+1)^2}. \tag{18}
\]
Combining (11), (14), (15), and (18) with
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^\star[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 \leq\frac{\Delta^2}{(\sqrt n+1)^2}
\]
from Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}hull\mbox{-}independent\mbox{-}affine\mbox{-}upper}\) proves, for \(n\in\{2,4,6\}\),
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}
 =\Delta^2\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}
 >\frac{\Delta^2}{(\sqrt n+1)^2}
 \geq\mathfrak R_n^\star. \tag{19}
\]

It remains to give the rational independent-design certificate at \(n=8\).  For integers \(k,\ell\geq0\) with \(k+\ell\leq8\), define
\[
 H_{k,\ell}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}2^{-\ell}\binom\ell j
 \left(d_{8,k+j}-\frac{2k+\ell}{8}\right)^2. \tag{20}
\]
This is the normalized shifted-binomial risk in Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}hull\mbox{-}bounded\mbox{-}global\mbox{-}reduction}\).  Every coordinate specified in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}n8\mbox{-}independent\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}certificate}\) lies in \([0,2]\), so \(d_8\) is feasible.  Put
\[
 D_0=2^{14}10^{12}=16384000000000000,
 \qquad \sigma_{k,\ell}=D_0(I_8-H_{k,\ell}). \tag{21}
\]
Substitution of the nine integer numerators of \(d_8\) into (20), followed by common-denominator arithmetic, gives the following exhaustive list.  Row \(k\) contains \(\sigma_{k,0},\ldots,\sigma_{k,8-k}\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
k&(\sigma_{k,0},\ldots,\sigma_{k,8-k})\\ \hline
0&(4577441792,3880130560,30789297309696,0,238862336,
53461707285504,105693419993088,97336380346880,3580346880)\\
1&(327965806819328,359818810488832,281843022690304,293958109724672,
358362791708672,371515404700672,283644940700672,97336380346880)\\
2&(660197382158336,530887778891776,581356140759040,631689073692672,
560408945692672,371515404700672,105693419993088)\\
3&(787093695625216,855369846626304,824582262626304,631689073692672,
358362791708672,53461707285504)\\
4&(985221165627392,855369846626304,581356140759040,293958109724672,
238862336)\\
5&(787093695625216,530887778891776,281843022690304,0)\\
6&(660197382158336,359818810488832,30789297309696)\\
7&(327965806819328,3880130560)\\
8&(4577441792).
\end{array} \tag{22}
\]
All entries in (22) are nonnegative, and the only zeros are at \((k,\ell)=(0,3)\) and \((5,3)\).  Because \(D_0>0\), (21)--(22) prove exactly that
\[
 \max_{\substack{k,\ell\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\\k+\ell\leq8}}H_{k,\ell}
 =I_8=\frac{481065022279}{8000000000000}, \tag{23}
\]
with precisely those two maximizers.  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}hull\mbox{-}bounded\mbox{-}global\mbox{-}reduction}\) applies to the feasible action \(d_8\): its measurable Bernstein extension has separately convex risk on the bounded cube, and its endpoint maximum is (23).  Therefore
\[
 \mathfrak R_8^\star[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 \leq\Delta^2 I_8. \tag{24}
\]

Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}n8\mbox{-}strict\mbox{-}separation}\) proves
\[
 C_8\leq\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}\leq U_8. \tag{25}
\]
Multiplying (25) by \(\Delta^2>0\) and using (11) gives the stated two-sided bounded-class bracket.  Exact subtraction of the rational values gives
\[
 C_8-I_8
 =\frac{1489964546219114077997554988878251203581}
 {282893788917485944245799445288000000000000}>0. \tag{26}
\]
Combining (11), (24), (25), and (26) proves
\[
 \mathfrak R_8^{\mathrm{bal}}
 =\Delta^2\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}
 \geq\Delta^2 C_8
 >\Delta^2I_8
 \geq\mathfrak R_8^\star. \tag{27}
\]
Equations (19) and (27) prove strict suboptimality at exactly the four claimed even sizes.  Since (25) has distinct endpoints \(C_8<U_8\), it does not identify \(\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}\).  None of the finite comparisons proves strictness for any even \(n\geq10\), a uniform statement, or an asymptotic rate or constant.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(n\geq 1\), let \(L_{\mathrm{bd}}<U_{\mathrm{bd}}\), and let \(\delta\) be any fixed probability law on \(\{0,1\}^n\).  Put \(\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}=U_{\mathrm{bd}}-L_{\mathrm{bd}}>0\).  For \(A,C\in[0,1]^n\), define
\[
 \tau(A,C)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(A_i-C_i),
 \qquad O_D(A,C)=\bigl(D_iA_i+(1-D_i)C_i\bigr)_{i=1}^n.
\]
Define the bounded-cube fixed-design minimax risk
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^\delta[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 :=\inf_{\widehat\tau\ {\rm measurable}}
 \sup_{\mathbf y\in[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]^{2n}}
 \sum_{D\in\{0,1\}^n}\delta(D)
 \left[\widehat\tau\bigl(D,(y_{iD_i})_{i=1}^n\bigr)
 -\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_{i1}-y_{i0})\right]^2,
\]
and define the labeled binary-endpoint minimax value
\[
 r_n^\delta
 :=\inf_{\{t_D:\{0,1\}^n\to[-1,1]\}_{D\in\{0,1\}^n}}
 \max_{(A,C)\in\{0,1\}^{2n}}
 \sum_{D\in\{0,1\}^n}\delta(D)
 \{t_D(O_D(A,C))-\tau(A,C)\}^2.
\]
Then
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^\delta[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 =\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2 r_n^\delta.
\]
In particular, if \(n\) is positive and even and \(\delta\) is uniform on \(\mathcal Z_n\), then
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 =\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}.
\]
This is an equality of minimax values for a fixed design; it does not assert that two success counts, or any other binary orbit statistic, are sufficient for nonbinary schedules.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix \(n\), \(L_{\mathrm{bd}}<U_{\mathrm{bd}}\), and \(\delta\) as in the statement, and abbreviate \(\Delta=\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}>0\).  Write every bounded schedule uniquely as
\[
 y_{i1}=L_{\mathrm{bd}}+\Delta A_i,
 \qquad y_{i0}=L_{\mathrm{bd}}+\Delta C_i,
 \qquad (A,C)\in[0,1]^{2n}.
\]
Its causal average treatment effect is
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_{i1}-y_{i0})
 =\frac{\Delta}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(A_i-C_i)
 =\Delta\tau(A,C). \tag{1}
\]
The positivity of \(\Delta\) justifies every normalization below.

We first prove the lower bound.  The target in (1) lies in \([-\Delta,\Delta]\), so projecting any estimator onto that closed interval cannot increase its squared error at any schedule.  Hence it is enough to consider bounded estimators.  Given such an estimator \(\widehat\tau\), restrict it to endpoint observations and define
\[
 t_D(b)=\Delta^{-1}\widehat\tau
 \bigl(D,(L_{\mathrm{bd}}+\Delta b_i)_{i=1}^n\bigr),
 \qquad b\in\{0,1\}^n.
\]
Then \(t_D(b)\in[-1,1]\).  At every endpoint schedule \((A,C)\in\{0,1\}^{2n}\), the observed normalized outcome vector is exactly \(O_D(A,C)\), and (1) gives the risk identity
\[
 \sum_D\delta(D)
 \left[\widehat\tau\bigl(D,(y_{iD_i})_i\bigr)
       -\frac1n\sum_i(y_{i1}-y_{i0})\right]^2
 =\Delta^2\sum_D\delta(D)
 \{t_D(O_D(A,C))-\tau(A,C)\}^2. \tag{2}
\]
The endpoint schedules are contained in the bounded cube.  Taking the maximum over endpoints in (2), then using the definition of \(r_n^\delta\), gives for every \(\widehat\tau\)
\[
 \sup_{(A,C)\in[0,1]^{2n}}R_{\widehat\tau}(A,C)
 \geq \Delta^2 r_n^\delta.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(\widehat\tau\) proves
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^\delta[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 \geq\Delta^2 r_n^\delta. \tag{3}
\]

For the reverse inequality, let \(\varepsilon>0\).  By the definition of the infimum \(r_n^\delta\), there is a deterministic family \(\{t_D^\varepsilon\}\), with every action in \([-1,1]\), whose maximum binary risk is at most \(r_n^\delta+\varepsilon\).  No attainment or compactness assertion is needed.  For \(z\in[0,1]^n\), form its tensor-product multilinear extension
\[
 \overline t_D^\varepsilon(z)
 =\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^n}t_D^\varepsilon(b)
   \prod_{i=1}^n z_i^{b_i}(1-z_i)^{1-b_i}. \tag{4}
\]
The coefficients in (4) are nonnegative and sum to
\(
 \prod_i\{z_i+(1-z_i)\}=1
\), so \(\overline t_D^\varepsilon(z)\in[-1,1]\).  Moreover, if \(z=b\in\{0,1\}^n\), all summands except the one indexed by \(b\) vanish, whence
\[
 \overline t_D^\varepsilon(b)=t_D^\varepsilon(b). \tag{5}
\]
Define the bounded-outcome estimator
\[
 \widehat\tau_\varepsilon
 \bigl(D,(y_{iD_i})_{i=1}^n\bigr)
 =\Delta\,\overline t_D^\varepsilon
 \left(\left(\frac{y_{iD_i}-L_{\mathrm{bd}}}{\Delta}\right)_{i=1}^n\right)
 =\Delta\,\overline t_D^\varepsilon(O_D(A,C)). \tag{6}
\]
For each fixed \(D\), (4) is a polynomial, and the assignment space is finite; hence (6) is measurable.

We now locate the maximum risk of (6).  Define its normalized error at assignment \(D\) by
\[
 e_D(A,C)=\overline t_D^\varepsilon(O_D(A,C))-\tau(A,C).
\]
Fix all coordinates except \(A_j\).  If \(D_j=1\), the multilinearity in (4) and the identity \(O_{D,j}=A_j\) show that the first term in \(e_D\) is affine in \(A_j\); if \(D_j=0\), that term is constant in \(A_j\).  In either case \(\tau(A,C)\) is affine in \(A_j\), so \(e_D(A,C)\) is affine in \(A_j\).  The same argument applies to \(C_j\): the first term is affine when \(D_j=0\) and constant when \(D_j=1\), while the target is affine.  Thus, for every assignment and every one of the \(2n\) potential-outcome coordinates, \(e_D\) is affine in that coordinate.  Its square is therefore convex in that coordinate, because if \(e_D(r)=\alpha r+\beta\), then
\[
 \frac{d^2}{dr^2}e_D(r)^2=2\alpha^2\geq0. \tag{7}
\]
The normalized assignment-averaged risk
\[
 Q_\varepsilon(A,C)=\sum_D\delta(D)e_D(A,C)^2
\]
is separately convex as a nonnegative weighted sum of the functions in (7); here \(\delta(D)\geq0\) and \(\sum_D\delta(D)=1\) because \(\delta\) is a probability law.

For completeness, separate convexity alone gives the required endpoint reduction.  If \(f\) is convex in one coordinate and that coordinate equals \(r\in[0,1]\), then
\[
 f(\ldots,r,\ldots)
 \leq(1-r)f(\ldots,0,\ldots)+r f(\ldots,1,\ldots)
 \leq\max_{c\in\{0,1\}}f(\ldots,c,\ldots). \tag{8}
\]
Applying (8) successively to all \(2n\) coordinates yields
\[
 \sup_{(A,C)\in[0,1]^{2n}}Q_\varepsilon(A,C)
 =\max_{(A,C)\in\{0,1\}^{2n}}Q_\varepsilon(A,C). \tag{9}
\]
Equality follows because the endpoint set on the right is a subset of the cube.  On that endpoint set, (5) identifies \(Q_\varepsilon\) with the binary risk of \(t^\varepsilon\).  Equations (6) and (9) therefore imply
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^\delta[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 \leq\Delta^2(r_n^\delta+\varepsilon).
\]
Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) and combining with (3) proves
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^\delta[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 =\Delta^2r_n^\delta. \tag{10}
\]

Finally suppose that \(n\) is positive and even and \(\delta\) is uniform on \(\mathcal Z_n\).  Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}response\mbox{-}type\mbox{-}minimax\mbox{-}games}\) proves, on the binary endpoint experiment, that permutation averaging loses no minimax value and that the resulting full-count game has value \(\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}\).  Hence \(r_n^\delta=\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}\), and (10) becomes
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 =\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}.
\]
Only this last binary identification uses the response-type orbit theorem; the extension (4)--(10) uses the full labeled observation and makes no nonbinary sufficiency claim.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
For every \(L_{\mathrm{bd}}<U_{\mathrm{bd}}\) and every positive even \(n\), balanced complete randomization has the exact bounded-cube minimax value
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 =\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}.
\]
Consequently, at the first three positive even sizes,
\[
 \mathfrak R_2^{\mathrm{bal}}=\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2}{4},
 \qquad
 \mathfrak R_4^{\mathrm{bal}}
 =\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right),
 \qquad
 \mathfrak R_6^{\mathrm{bal}}=\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2s_6^2,
\]
where all risks have arguments \([L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]\).  At \(n=8\),
\[
 \Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2C_8
 \leq\mathfrak R_8^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 =\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}
 \leq\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2U_8.
\]
For every \(n\in\{2,4,6,8\}\), balanced complete randomization is strictly suboptimal in Hull's class of all bounded schedules and all measurable estimators:
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^\star[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]
 <\mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}].
\]
For \(n\in\{2,4,6\}\), the certificate is
\[
 \mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}
 =\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}
 >\frac{\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2}{(\sqrt n+1)^2}
 \geq\mathfrak R_n^\star.
\]
At \(n=8\), the certificate is
\[
 \mathfrak R_8^{\mathrm{bal}}
 \geq\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2C_8
 >\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2I_8
 \geq\mathfrak R_8^\star.
\]
The independent-design endpoint action \(d_8\) has normalized worst-case risk exactly \(I_8\), attained only at Hull states \((k,\ell)=(0,3)\) and \((5,3)\).  The exact value of \(\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}\), every comparison for even \(n\geq10\), Hull's uniform-in-\(n\) strict-suboptimality conjecture, and every asymptotic rate or constant remain open.

The replacement records the exact balanced-design minimax value, its exact consequences at two, four, and six, and its certified bracket at eight while leaving the exact eight-unit value and all later-even or asymptotic claims open.

 \mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]

proposed.justification: The fixed-design endpoint equality converts the exact binary balanced-design saddles into exact bounded-cube risks at two, four, and six and converts the eight-unit binary certificates into a bounded-cube bracket.
proposed.gap: Hull's uniform complete-randomization conjecture remains open; the theorem proves strict comparison only at four finite even sizes and does not determine the exact eight-unit balanced risk.
proposed.consumer: Designers choosing between exact balance and independent half assignment obtain exact bounded-cube worst-case MSE values at two, four, and six and a certified bracket and strict comparison at eight.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The theorem must depend on the new fixed-design endpoint lemma and record the exact value equality and finite consequences required by the active directive.

proposed_core_edits.proposed: The primary binary fixed-design functional is \(\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}=\min_t\max_{N\in\mathcal N_n}\sum_{x,y}K_N(x,y)\{t(x,y)-\tau_N\}^2\). For every fixed assignment law \(\delta\), the bounded-cube minimax ATE functional equals \(\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2\) times its labeled binary-endpoint fixed-design minimax functional. In particular, under uniform balanced complete randomization, \(\mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{bal}}[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]=\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2\rho_n^{\mathrm{CR}}\) for every positive even \(n\). The globally optimized comparator \(\mathfrak R_n^\star[L_{\mathrm{bd}},U_{\mathrm{bd}}]\) additionally takes an infimum over all assignment designs and all measurable estimators.
proposed_core_edits.reason: The new fixed-design endpoint theorem upgrades a one-sided endpoint lower bound to an exact relation between the bounded and binary minimax functionals, so the headline functional metadata must state that relation.

prose_updates.tldr: Exact balance removes treatment-share variation but leaves two observed arm-success counts. For fixed binary potential outcomes, the full pair and its difference have equal worst-schedule ATE squared-error minimax risk at \(n=2,4,6\), but a rational two-sided full-count bracket and a difference-only lower certificate prove strict loss at \(n=8\). A tensor-product endpoint extension separately proves that, for any fixed assignment law, bounded-cube minimax ATE risk equals \(\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2\) times the corresponding labeled binary-endpoint minimax value. Thus balanced complete randomization has exact bounded-cube risks \(\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2/4\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2(1-\sqrt3/2)\), and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2s_6^2\) at two, four, and six, and a certified \(\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2[C_8,U_8]\) bracket at eight; it is strictly worse than Hull's globally optimized independent design at all four sizes. Later-even compression persistence, the exact eight-unit value, Hull's uniform strictness conjecture, and all asymptotic laws remain open.

project_justification.fill: The project gives analytic equality saddles at \(n=2,4,6\), rational lower and upper full-count certificates and strict count-compression separation at eight, and a fixed-design tensor-product endpoint theorem equating bounded-cube minimax risk with the scaled labeled binary-endpoint value. The latter yields exact balanced-design bounded risks at two, four, and six, a certified bracket at eight, and strict comparison with Hull's globally optimized independent design at those four sizes.

prose_updates.related_work: Hull (2026, Theorem 1 and Appendix A.4) optimizes worst-case ATE squared error jointly over all bounded schedules, assignment designs, and measurable estimators, proves that independent half assignment attains the shifted-binomial minimax program, and uses Bernstein extension plus separate convexity to lift endpoint risks to the full bounded cube. Corollary 1 gives the affine independent-design risk \(\Delta_{\mathrm{bd}}^2/(\sqrt n+1)^2\); footnote 12 records uniform strict suboptimality of complete randomization with general estimators as a conjecture supported numerically. Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}fixed\mbox{-}design\mbox{-}endpoint\mbox{-}reduction}\) gives a distinct fixed-design minimax-value equality by extending the complete labeled binary rule, without asserting a nonbinary orbit statistic. Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}hull\mbox{-}class\mbox{-}complete\mbox{-}randomization\mbox{-}strict\mbox{-}small\mbox{-}n}\) combines that equality with finite certificates to prove Hull's strict comparison only for \(n=2,4,6,8\), leaving the uniform conjecture open. Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026) study the unrestricted independent-design scalar program and its Airy expansion, not the exact balanced hypergeometric count-compression threshold. Ding and Dasgupta (2016) supply the binary response types and observed table used in the finite kernel. Blackwell (1953) gives only weak dominance of the full count pair over its difference. Bai (2023) treats permutation-invariant linear procedures. Rigdon and Hudgens (2015), Li and Ding (2016), and Li and Ding (2017) concern exact confidence sets or first-order finite-population limits and do not imply the point-estimation or bounded-design claims here.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The rational full-count certificates at \(n=8\) prove only \(C_8\leq\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}\leq U_8\), with \(C_8<U_8\), so the exact binary and bounded-cube balanced minimax values remain unknown. An arbitrary prior can make the second count Bayes-informative even where the minimax values agree. The fixed-design endpoint result is an equality of minimax values obtained by tensor-product extension of a full labeled binary rule; it does not prove that two counts, or any other binary orbit statistic, suffice for nonbinary schedules.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The theorem-level scope consists of the exact binary response-type games, equality of full-count and difference-only risks at \(n=2,4,6\), strict count-compression separation and a two-sided full-count bracket at \(n=8\), the resulting first-lossy-size conclusion, the fixed-design endpoint minimax-value reduction, exact bounded-cube balanced risks at two, four, and six, a bounded-cube bracket at eight, and strict suboptimality of balanced complete randomization relative to the globally optimized design at those four sizes. The paper makes no confidence-set claim, pointwise-dominance claim, exact \(\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}\) claim, or nonbinary two-count sufficiency claim. Strict count-compression persistence for even \(n\geq10\), Hull's uniform complete-randomization conjecture, and every asymptotic rate, exponent, parity law, or constant for the balance or compression tax remain open.

statement_notes.justification: A fixed-design tensor-product endpoint argument upgrades the endpoint-subclass lower bound to exact minimax-value equality, so the finite binary saddles now give exact bounded-cube balanced risks at two, four, and six and a two-sided bracket at eight.
statement_notes.gap: Hull's all-design theorem and numerical conjecture do not give these exact fixed-design values. The present result proves strict suboptimality only at four finite even sizes and leaves the exact eight-unit value and uniform conjecture open.
statement_notes.consumer: Users of \(\operatorname{complete\_ra}\) obtain exact worst-case bounded-outcome MSE values at two, four, and six and a certified bracket and strict independent-design comparison at eight.
